newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore dollar gains seen capped for time being.
newsitem.headline: Singapore dollar gains seen capped for time being.

text.p: Comments by Singapore's finance minister favouring a stronger Singapore dollar are unlikely to have a sustained impact in the face of a surging U.S. dollar and relatively subdued inflation, economists said on Wednesday.
In an interview in the Financial Times' Wednesday edition, Finance Minister Richard Hu was quoted as saying some strengthening of the Singapore dollar would be desirable to keep inflation down.
"Some degree of appreciation is desirable from our point of view because we import 70 percent of all the goods we consume," Hu said.
The local currency started just below S$1.4100 to the U.S. dollar on Wednesday morning and rose to S$1.4060 on the back of the report.
But forex dealers said active buying of the U.S. unit by local banks around the S$1.4060 level sparked speculation of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).
The MAS, the de facto central bank, typically intervenes in forex markets through major local banks to stem any sharp moves in the domestic currency.
The local unit was quoted near S$1.4080 to the U.S. dollar in late Asian trade.
"It was more a knee-jerk reaction. It's just the speculative traders who would jump on this," said a senior dealer at a Thai bank in Singapore.
"If the dollar/majors choose to climb like this, they've got no choice but to let the Sing dollar weaken because an ultra-strong Sing would be bad for investment here and for our exports," he added.
The U.S. dollar surged to 122.60/70 yen in late Asian trading against a New York overnight close of 120.95/21.03.
The Singapore dollar appreciated by a subdued 1.2 percent against the U.S. dollar last year after posting a near-three percent rise in 1995.
"As long as inflation is not threatening, (the authorities) would be quite happy to see a stable Sing dollar," said Lim Bok Eng, regional economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

He said inflation was expected to be higher this year than in 1996, but was unlikely to climb above three percent, reducing the need for the authorities to endorse a sharply stronger Singapore dollar.
While Singapore's sound economic fundamentals inevitably led to an appreciation of the currency over time, Lim said the scope for such rises looked limited.
"Against the background of a surging U.S. dollar, the Singapore dollar will struggle to achieve many gains at the moment," said Desmond Supple, senior economist at independent research firm I.D.E.A.
While the Singapore dollar has remained relatively steady against the U.S. unit, it has strengthened sharply against the Japanese yen over the past year, he said.
The Singapore dollar's 18 percent appreciation against the yen since the end of 1995 had helped control import prices as Japan is Singapore's largest supplier of imports.

"In terms of imported inflation, there is no real risk at the moment," Supple said, adding that lower import costs also helped underpin Singapore's export competitiveness as imports played a major role in the production process.
